items.summary: The Medicare Spending Per Beneficiary (MSPB) Measure shows whether Medicare spends more, less, or about the same for an episode of care (episode) at a specific hospital compared to all hospitals nationally. An MSPB episode includes Medicare Part A and Part B payments for services provided by hospitals and other healthcare providers the 3 days prior to, during, and 30 days following a patient's inpatient stay. This measure evaluates hospitals' costs compared to the costs of the national median (or midpoint) hospital. This measure takes into account important factors like patient age and health status (risk adjustment) and geographic payment differences (payment-standardization).

Many healthcare associated infections can be prevented when the hospitals use CDC-recommended infection control steps.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Hospital General Information
story_ideas.headline: Look up your nearest hospital's overall rating before you need it
story_ideas.angle: A county-level walkthrough of the Medicare-registered hospital list, with hospital type and overall rating, for older adults who have one realistic hospital within driving distance.
story_ideas.hook: The file that names every hospital registered with Medicare, with addresses, type and overall rating, was reissued on 10/26/26 and breaks to states and counties.
story_ideas.summary: A list of all hospitals that have been registered with Medicare. The list includes addresses, phone numbers, hospital type, and overall hospital rating.
story_ideas.consumer: Pull the entry for the hospital you would be taken to, note its type and overall rating, and check whether the next-nearest one is rated differently before an emergency makes the choice for you.
story_ideas.b2b: For post-acute and senior living operators, the type-and-rating field is the cleanest public map of which referral sources in a market are rated above or below their neighbors.
story_ideas.localize: Breaks down to US states, US counties — rank the outliers.
story_ideas.competitive: Reference data — a refreshed file, so no coverage claim applies either way.
story_ideas.why: If you only learn your hospital's rating after admission, you have lost the one moment when the information could have changed where you went.
story_ideas.note: Localizable to US states and counties; supports a sortable table and metro-level cuts.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Medicare Spending Per Beneficiary - Hospital
story_ideas.headline: What Medicare spends on the thirty days after your hospital stay, hospital by hospital
story_ideas.angle: A piece comparing hospitals on the MSPB episode, which covers Part A and Part B payments from three days before admission through 30 days after discharge, for families planning what happens after a hospital stay.
story_ideas.hook: The measure is explicitly an episode, not a stay, so a hospital's number reflects the care chain it discharges people into.
story_ideas.consumer: Ask the discharge planner what happens in the 30 days after you leave, and compare the hospital's spending-per-episode standing against hospitals nationally before you agree to a post-acute placement.
story_ideas.b2b: Hospitals carrying high episode spending have the strongest incentive to tighten their post-acute networks, which decides which skilled nursing and home health providers keep referrals.
story_ideas.why: The thirty days after discharge is where readmissions and unplanned costs land, and this is the only public figure that puts a hospital's whole episode in one number.
story_ideas.note: State and county geography; pairs naturally with the readmissions file for a two-measure chart.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Unplanned Hospital Visits - Hospital
story_ideas.headline: How often patients end up back in the hospital after they are sent home
story_ideas.angle: A readmissions and return-days explainer built from the provider-level file, for families weighing a discharge date they feel is too early.
story_ideas.hook: The file carries excess days in acute care, unplanned readmissions and unplanned visits after outpatient procedures in one provider-level record, refreshed 10/20/26.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you accept a discharge plan, look up the hospital's unplanned return record and ask what support is arranged for the first week at home.
story_ideas.b2b: Operators taking referrals from a hospital with heavy return days are taking on the clinical risk that shows up in that hospital's numbers.
story_ideas.why: A second admission within weeks is the most common way a short stay turns into a long-term care decision, and the pattern is on the public record before it happens to you.
story_ideas.note: Provider level with state and county rollups; strong candidate for a metro ranking.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Healthcare Associated Infections - Hospital
story_ideas.headline: The infections patients pick up in the hospital are on the public record
story_ideas.angle: A hospital-by-hospital read of the CDC-developed infection measures collected through the National Healthcare Safety Network, for older patients facing a planned admission with a central line or catheter.
story_ideas.hook: The measures cover device-related infections that occur while a patient is in the hospital and are reported at provider level, refreshed 10/19/26.
story_ideas.consumer: If a procedure is scheduled, ask which devices will be used and check the hospital's infection measures for those device types first.
story_ideas.b2b: Infection performance at referring hospitals shapes what post-acute providers inherit on admission and what they will be held to afterward.
story_ideas.why: Device-related infection is one of the few hospital risks a patient can weigh in advance, and the measure exists specifically so they can.
story_ideas.note: CDC-developed measures via NHSN; county and state cuts available.;

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Patient survey (HCAHPS) - Hospital
story_ideas.headline: What other patients said about the hospital you are being sent to
story_ideas.angle: A read of the national standardized inpatient survey at hospital level, for families choosing between two hospitals in the same market.
story_ideas.hook: HCAHPS is a national, standardized survey of recent inpatients, which makes hospital-to-hospital comparison fair in a way that online reviews are not.
story_ideas.consumer: Compare the survey results for the two hospitals nearest you, and weigh them against the travel time you would have to accept to reach the better-rated one.
story_ideas.b2b: Survey standing is a marketing asset and a referral filter, and it moves with staffing levels operators are already struggling to hold.
story_ideas.why: Patient experience is the part of hospital quality a family can verify independently, and the survey is the only version of it collected the same way everywhere.
story_ideas.note: Refreshed 10/19/26; state and county geography supports local comparison tables.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Inpatient Psychiatric Facility Quality Measure Data - by State
story_ideas.headline: Your state's record on psychiatric hospital discharges, in one file
story_ideas.angle: A state-level comparison of IPFQR measures including transition record, medication continuation and readmissions, for families of older adults admitted for behavioral health care.
story_ideas.hook: The state file puts transition-record, screening-for-metabolic-disorders and medication continuation measures side by side across states, refreshed 10/19/26.
story_ideas.consumer: If an older relative is admitted to an inpatient psychiatric facility, ask for the transition record at discharge and whether medications will be continued, both of which your state is measured on.
story_ideas.b2b: Behavioral health discharge quality determines how often older patients arrive at senior living and skilled nursing without a usable medication plan.
story_ideas.why: A discharge without a transition record or continued medication is the most preventable way a psychiatric admission turns into the next one.
story_ideas.note: State level with matching facility and national files for a three-tier chart.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Facility Affiliation Data
story_ideas.headline: Find out which hospitals and facilities your doctor is actually tied to
story_ideas.angle: A how-to on the publicly reported facility affiliations file for patients who assume their physician follows them wherever they are admitted.
story_ideas.hook: The affiliations data is published in the Provider Data Catalog and was reissued 10/30/26, making the clinician-to-facility link checkable without asking anyone.
story_ideas.consumer: Look up your doctor's affiliations before you choose a hospital or a nursing home, so you know whether the person who knows your history will be there.
story_ideas.b2b: Affiliation patterns are the clearest public evidence of which physician groups anchor which facilities in a market, which matters in any referral or acquisition conversation.
story_ideas.why: Continuity of the clinician who knows your medication list is often the difference between a smooth admission and a reconstructed one.
story_ideas.note: Pairs with the clinician National Downloadable File, reissued 10/30/26, for a market-level view.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Consumer Price Index, medical care, October 2026 — 595.47 index 1982-84=100
story_ideas.headline: Medical prices and your 2027 raise are not moving at the same speed
story_ideas.angle: A side-by-side of the October 2026 medical care CPI at 595.47 against the 3.6 percent Social Security cost-of-living increase effective December 2026, for retirees budgeting next year.
story_ideas.hook: Two federal numbers published weeks apart set the ceiling on what an older household can absorb next year, and nobody publishes them together.
story_ideas.consumer: Work out what share of your current benefit goes to medical costs, then apply the 3.6 percent increase to the whole check and see what is left over.
story_ideas.b2b: Advisors and insurers selling retirement income products are planning against a medical price series that does not track the benefit adjustment their clients receive.
story_ideas.chart: The underlying file supports an original ranking or trend line.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: If medical spending is a large share of your budget, a percentage raise on the whole benefit is smaller in practice than it looks on paper.
story_ideas.note: National only; the COLA figure comes from the 10/26/26 Federal Register determination.

story_ideas.title: Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for 2027
story_ideas.headline: Social Security rises 3.6 percent in December, and the wage index moved too
story_ideas.angle: A plain reading of the 2027 determinations notice, including the 3.6 percent benefit increase effective December 2026 and the 2025 national average wage index of $72,800.33, for people near claiming age.
story_ideas.hook: The same notice that sets the benefit increase also resets the wage index that drives other program parameters, which rarely gets explained to the people it affects.
story_ideas.consumer: Check what the 3.6 percent increase does to your own benefit from December 2026, and if you are still working, note that the 2025 average wage index is $72,800.33.
story_ideas.b2b: Wage-index movement feeds the program parameters that retirement product pricing and employer benefit modeling rest on.
story_ideas.why: Knowing the exact increase and effective month lets you budget from a real number instead of a headline percentage.
story_ideas.note: Federal Register notice of 10/26/26; national figures, no state breakout.

story_ideas.title: Medicaid Waiver Tracker: Approved and Pending Section 1115 Waivers by State
story_ideas.headline: Check whether your state has asked to change Medicaid's rules
story_ideas.angle: A state-by-state read of approved and pending Section 1115 waiver provisions covering eligibility, benefits and delivery-system changes, for families whose long-term care depends on Medicaid.
story_ideas.hook: The tracker was updated 11/13/26 and shows both expansions and restrictions pending, which means today's eligibility rules are not necessarily next year's.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** The second year of the rural health fund is paying out at wildly different rates depending on which side of a state line a person lives on, and the files that describe the hospitals those people actually use were all refreshed in the same three weeks. KFF's analysis, posted 11/13/26, puts awards per rural resident below $100 in twelve states and above $500 in eight. CMS reissued Hospital General Information on 10/26/26, Medicare Spending Per Beneficiary - Hospital, Healthcare Associated Infections and the HCAHPS patient survey on 10/19/26, and Unplanned Hospital Visits on 10/20/26, each carrying state and county geography. Set side by side, they let a state's per-resident award be read against the named hospitals in that state and the Medicare record those hospitals already carry: episode spending from three days before admission through thirty days after discharge, infection rates, readmissions, and what discharged patients said.

**Why it matters:** A rural resident in one of the twelve states under $100 per head is usually the person with the fewest alternatives if the one hospital within reach thins its services. Nothing in the award figures tells that person anything about their own hospital. The CMS files do, down to the county, and they are the only public record in this run that answers the question a rural family actually asks: is the place I would be taken to any good, and what happens in the thirty days after they send me home. The five-to-one spread is the national story; the hospital-level files are what makes it usable.

**Why pitch this now:** The second-year award analysis published 11/13/26, the day of this run, and it is the first look at how year two differs from year one. The CMS hospital files refreshed between 10/19/26 and 10/26/26 and the survey-based ones replace the oldest quarter with the most recently completed one, so the current numbers are live and will be overwritten at the next quarterly update.

**Angle:** Whether the second year of rural health money is reaching the states whose hospitals carry the heaviest Medicare episode spending and readmission records, and what a rural family can learn about its own hospital from the October files while the question is argued at the state level. Working title: "The Hundred-Dollar States." For rural older adults and their families, and for the post-acute operators whose referrals come from those hospitals.

**Potential headlines:**
- Twelve states got less than $100 per rural resident this year
- Your rural hospital's Medicare record is public, county by county
- Rural health dollars stop at the state line

**Potential outlets:**
- **USA Today** — the award figures break to the state level and the hospital files to the county, which is exactly the shape the Gannett locals in low-award states can run.
- **Next Avenue** — writes aging from the reader's side, and this is a piece about what an older person in a thinly served county can look up before an ambulance ride decides it for them.
- **Skilled Nursing News** — rural skilled nursing depends on referrals from the same hospitals whose readmission and episode-spending numbers just refreshed.
- **Modern Healthcare** — a national policy readership that will want the year-two award spread set against hospital-level Medicare spending rather than reported on its own.

I would like to write the version a reader in one of the low-award states can actually use. CMS refreshed its hospital files in late October: Hospital General Information on 10/26/26, Medicare Spending Per Beneficiary, Healthcare Associated Infections and the HCAHPS patient survey on 10/19/26, Unplanned Hospital Visits on 10/20/26. All carry state and county identifiers. Setting the award figures beside the named hospitals in each state gives a piece that reads nationally and breaks apart cleanly for local newsrooms: about 1,200 words plus a sortable state table. USA Today reaches the rural readers in those twelve states, and they are the ones living furthest from a second hospital if the first one narrows what it offers.
pitch_ideas_raw:
**Look up your nearest hospital's overall rating before you need it**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Hospital General Information*  
- Angle: A county-level walkthrough of the Medicare-registered hospital list, with hospital type and overall rating, for older adults who have one realistic hospital within driving distance.
- Hook: The file that names every hospital registered with Medicare, with addresses, type and overall rating, was reissued on 10/26/26 and breaks to states and counties.
- For readers: Pull the entry for the hospital you would be taken to, note its type and overall rating, and check whether the next-nearest one is rated differently before an emergency makes the choice for you.
- For the trade: For post-acute and senior living operators, the type-and-rating field is the cleanest public map of which referral sources in a market are rated above or below their neighbors.
- Why it matters: If you only learn your hospital's rating after admission, you have lost the one moment when the information could have changed where you went.
- Also: Localizable to US states and counties; supports a sortable table and metro-level cuts.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Fierce Healthcare

**What Medicare spends on the thirty days after your hospital stay, hospital by hospital**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Medicare Spending Per Beneficiary - Hospital*  
- Angle: A piece comparing hospitals on the MSPB episode, which covers Part A and Part B payments from three days before admission through 30 days after discharge, for families planning what happens after a hospital stay.
- Hook: The measure is explicitly an episode, not a stay, so a hospital's number reflects the care chain it discharges people into.
- For readers: Ask the discharge planner what happens in the 30 days after you leave, and compare the hospital's spending-per-episode standing against hospitals nationally before you agree to a post-acute placement.
- For the trade: Hospitals carrying high episode spending have the strongest incentive to tighten their post-acute networks, which decides which skilled nursing and home health providers keep referrals.
- Why it matters: The thirty days after discharge is where readmissions and unplanned costs land, and this is the only public figure that puts a hospital's whole episode in one number.
- Also: State and county geography; pairs naturally with the readmissions file for a two-measure chart.
- Pitch to: Modern Healthcare, Bankrate Retirement

**How often patients end up back in the hospital after they are sent home**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Unplanned Hospital Visits - Hospital*  
- Angle: A readmissions and return-days explainer built from the provider-level file, for families weighing a discharge date they feel is too early.
- Hook: The file carries excess days in acute care, unplanned readmissions and unplanned visits after outpatient procedures in one provider-level record, refreshed 10/20/26.
- For readers: Before you accept a discharge plan, look up the hospital's unplanned return record and ask what support is arranged for the first week at home.
- For the trade: Operators taking referrals from a hospital with heavy return days are taking on the clinical risk that shows up in that hospital's numbers.
- Why it matters: A second admission within weeks is the most common way a short stay turns into a long-term care decision, and the pattern is on the public record before it happens to you.
- Also: Provider level with state and county rollups; strong candidate for a metro ranking.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Long-Term Care News, Skilled Nursing News

**The infections patients pick up in the hospital are on the public record**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Healthcare Associated Infections - Hospital*  
- Angle: A hospital-by-hospital read of the CDC-developed infection measures collected through the National Healthcare Safety Network, for older patients facing a planned admission with a central line or catheter.
- Hook: The measures cover device-related infections that occur while a patient is in the hospital and are reported at provider level, refreshed 10/19/26.
- For readers: If a procedure is scheduled, ask which devices will be used and check the hospital's infection measures for those device types first.
- For the trade: Infection performance at referring hospitals shapes what post-acute providers inherit on admission and what they will be held to afterward.
- Why it matters: Device-related infection is one of the few hospital risks a patient can weigh in advance, and the measure exists specifically so they can.
- Also: CDC-developed measures via NHSN; county and state cuts available.;
- Pitch to: Skilled Nursing News, Family Caregiver Alliance

**What other patients said about the hospital you are being sent to**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Patient survey (HCAHPS) - Hospital*  
- Angle: A read of the national standardized inpatient survey at hospital level, for families choosing between two hospitals in the same market.
- Hook: HCAHPS is a national, standardized survey of recent inpatients, which makes hospital-to-hospital comparison fair in a way that online reviews are not.
- For readers: Compare the survey results for the two hospitals nearest you, and weigh them against the travel time you would have to accept to reach the better-rated one.
- For the trade: Survey standing is a marketing asset and a referral filter, and it moves with staffing levels operators are already struggling to hold.
- Why it matters: Patient experience is the part of hospital quality a family can verify independently, and the survey is the only version of it collected the same way everywhere.
- Also: Refreshed 10/19/26; state and county geography supports local comparison tables.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Long-Term Care News, Bankrate Retirement

**Your state's record on psychiatric hospital discharges, in one file**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Inpatient Psychiatric Facility Quality Measure Data - by State*  
- Angle: A state-level comparison of IPFQR measures including transition record, medication continuation and readmissions, for families of older adults admitted for behavioral health care.
- Hook: The state file puts transition-record, screening-for-metabolic-disorders and medication continuation measures side by side across states, refreshed 10/19/26.
- For readers: If an older relative is admitted to an inpatient psychiatric facility, ask for the transition record at discharge and whether medications will be continued, both of which your state is measured on.
- For the trade: Behavioral health discharge quality determines how often older patients arrive at senior living and skilled nursing without a usable medication plan.
- Why it matters: A discharge without a transition record or continued medication is the most preventable way a psychiatric admission turns into the next one.
- Also: State level with matching facility and national files for a three-tier chart.
- Pitch to: Fierce Healthcare, SeniorLiving.org

**Find out which hospitals and facilities your doctor is actually tied to**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Facility Affiliation Data*  
- Angle: A how-to on the publicly reported facility affiliations file for patients who assume their physician follows them wherever they are admitted.
- Hook: The affiliations data is published in the Provider Data Catalog and was reissued 10/30/26, making the clinician-to-facility link checkable without asking anyone.
- For readers: Look up your doctor's affiliations before you choose a hospital or a nursing home, so you know whether the person who knows your history will be there.
- For the trade: Affiliation patterns are the clearest public evidence of which physician groups anchor which facilities in a market, which matters in any referral or acquisition conversation.
- Why it matters: Continuity of the clinician who knows your medication list is often the difference between a smooth admission and a reconstructed one.
- Also: Pairs with the clinician National Downloadable File, reissued 10/30/26, for a market-level view.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Long-Term Care News, Skilled Nursing News

**Medical prices and your 2027 raise are not moving at the same speed**
*BLS: Consumer Price Index, medical care, October 2026 — 595.47 index 1982-84=100*  
- Angle: A side-by-side of the October 2026 medical care CPI at 595.47 against the 3.6 percent Social Security cost-of-living increase effective December 2026, for retirees budgeting next year.
- Hook: Two federal numbers published weeks apart set the ceiling on what an older household can absorb next year, and nobody publishes them together.
- For readers: Work out what share of your current benefit goes to medical costs, then apply the 3.6 percent increase to the whole check and see what is left over.
- For the trade: Advisors and insurers selling retirement income products are planning against a medical price series that does not track the benefit adjustment their clients receive.
- Why it matters: If medical spending is a large share of your budget, a percentage raise on the whole benefit is smaller in practice than it looks on paper.
- Also: National only; the COLA figure comes from the 10/26/26 Federal Register determination.
- Pitch to: Bankrate Retirement, Forbes Retirement

**Social Security rises 3.6 percent in December, and the wage index moved too**
*Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for 2027*  
- Angle: A plain reading of the 2027 determinations notice, including the 3.6 percent benefit increase effective December 2026 and the 2025 national average wage index of $72,800.33, for people near claiming age.
- Hook: The same notice that sets the benefit increase also resets the wage index that drives other program parameters, which rarely gets explained to the people it affects.
- For readers: Check what the 3.6 percent increase does to your own benefit from December 2026, and if you are still working, note that the 2025 average wage index is $72,800.33.
- For the trade: Wage-index movement feeds the program parameters that retirement product pricing and employer benefit modeling rest on.
- Why it matters: Knowing the exact increase and effective month lets you budget from a real number instead of a headline percentage.
- Also: Federal Register notice of 10/26/26; national figures, no state breakout.
- Pitch to: Bankrate Retirement, Kiplinger
